extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity officers, and readers interested in retractions and scientific integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for evaluating image integrity in biomedical publications and procedures around institutional review and journal retraction when image manipulation is detected. Includes examples of unacceptable manipulations and commentary on tools/methods for image forensics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable image adjustment practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Image data must not be modified in ways that fall outside acceptable image adjustment practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices state image data 'appeared to be modified in ways determined to fall outside acceptable image adjustment practices.' Examples given: 'Fig. 1H appears to have examples of minor adjustments in cell location,' 'Fig. 3H appears to include examples of different layers added to the final image.' Such modifications are treated as unacceptable and can lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific problematic manipulations (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of manipulations are explicitly flagged as problematic evidence of data integrity breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted instances include 'areas of c-kit-positive staining selectively inserted into the image plane,' 'areas of c-kit-positive staining selectively added,' and 'the translocation of cells within the image.' Layering, selective insertion/addition of staining, and moving cells within images are cited as concrete examples of unacceptable manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional image-review findings as basis for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may retract papers based on the recommendation of an institution after that institution's review of image/data integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both notices begin 'based on the recommendation of Harvard Medical School (HMS) and Brigham and Woman’s Hospital (BWH), we are retracting this paper.' The institutional review of images served as the factual basis for the editors' decision to retract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should provide detailed, figure-level explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices are expected to describe the specific nature and location of problematic data (e.g., which figures and what was wrong) rather than issuing only a generic retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example notices identify particular figures and subpanels (e.g., 'Fig. 1A (Top Left)') and describe the precise concerns. This level of specificity communicates the reasons for retraction and the scope of the problems to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and dissemination of computational methods for investigating questioned data
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and share computer/software methods to examine large collections of images and other data when researching suspected misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comment notes that HMS published software for looking at large collections of images and that ORI announced funding for a conference on computer methods for examining questioned data. The page (via the comment) recommends dissemination of investigation methods and tools as a service to research and to aid large-scale inspections of image evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should notify journals and request withdrawal when integrity concerns exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When institutional reviews raise concerns about integrity, institutions should inform journals and may request that affected papers be pulled or retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post reports that 'Harvard has requested journals pull' papers over concerns about integrity and that journals acted on HMS/BWH recommendations. The practice of notifying journals is presented as part of the process, though the post also notes that such actions can provoke legal pushback from authors (as with lawsuits).
